title: Inflation reports
measures: How fast prices of a basket of goods and services are rising, usually compared with a month earlier and a year earlier. Many reports also show a 'core' figure that leaves out the most changeable items, such as food and energy.
whyItMatters: Central banks try to keep inflation near a target, so inflation figures shape expectations about interest rates. Those expectations feed into currencies, bond yields, stock valuations and commodities.
expectations: Forecasters publish a consensus figure before the release. Traders compare the actual number with that consensus, and with the previous figure, which is sometimes revised.
surprises: A figure above or below the consensus may change what traders expect the central bank to do. The headline and core figures can point different ways, and a revision to last month can matter as much as the new number. The first move can fade if the surprise was small or already expected by many traders.
limits: An inflation surprise does not set a price direction. A higher figure can strengthen a currency in one situation and weaken it in another, depending on what was priced in and how the central bank is expected to respond.
